title: How Building with AI Can Double the Throughput of Your Engineering Team — Brian Scanlan, Intercom

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is deploying Claude Code as an IDE/PR coding agent to transform Intercom's software development lifecycle, covering auto-approval of PRs, code review workflows, and engineering throughput metrics. Claude Code is an IDE and PR coding assistant, and the talk describes building internal plugins, skills, hooks, and platform infrastructure around it for software builders. Intercom deployed Claude Code in production engineering workflows and operates it at organizational scale with Honeycomb observability, compliance controls, and continuous skill improvement. Requires familiarity with software engineering practices, PR workflows, and organizational change management but remains accessible to a broad technical audience. A real-world case study presenting Intercom's quantitative results from deploying Claude Code across its engineering organization. Multiple transcript evidence anchors with quantitative metrics directly support the coding agents classification.

summary: Brian Scanlan contextualizes Intercom as a 15-year-old Irish-American B2B SaaS company that pivoted to AI, with its customer support agent Finn serving over 8,000 customers and revenue approaching $100 million. As a senior principal engineer on the platform group, he focuses on uptime, performance, security, and developer productivity for their Ruby on Rails monolith. After experimenting with GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Augment, Intercom set an ambitious goal: double engineering throughput in one year, measured as code changes per R&D person. The initiative required decisive leadership—updating job descriptions to make AI adoption mandatory, celebrating wins, running hackathons, and staffing a full-time 2x team. Intercom chose Claude Code as its single platform rather than letting engineers pick favorite tools, comparing multi-tool fragmentation to multi-cloud downsides. Their vision was to treat Claude like a senior engineer connected to everything an engineer can access, onboarded with Rails conventions, architecture, testing standards, and security rules, encapsulated in skills, captures, guidance, and hooks. Intercom's technically conservative culture favors using single tools extremely well, so they focus on small, high-quality, durable, testable skills with continuous improvement and backtesting against their huge body of historical code changes and incidents. A key principle is giving agents problems, not tasks—letting the agent figure out which skills to invoke. Brian illustrates this with a security incident where Claude automatically discovered and used a skill for data breach analysis he didn't know existed, completing in two minutes what would have taken twenty. Results after going all in on one tool starting in January: PR throughput doubled in under a year, 17.6% of PRs auto-approved with SOC 2, ISO 27001, and HIPAA compliance, code review becoming the new bottleneck, defects closing faster than ever, and Stanford research confirming code quality is increasing. The CI infrastructure melted under the volume. Claude Code has gone viral outside software engineering at Intercom, with hundreds of contributors to internal plugins. Brian frames the shift as analogous to sysadmin-to-SRE during cloud adoption but 100x faster, and notes single-person team experiments and using skills as a product manager.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Intercom Background
sections.summary: Brian introduces himself and Intercom: a 15-year-old Irish-American B2B SaaS company with ~1,400 employees, pivoted to AI. He covers revenue growth outperforming public SaaS peers and his role as senior principal engineer on the platform group managing the Rails monolith, uptime, security, and developer productivity.

sections.title: Intercom as an AI Company and Finn
sections.summary: Brian describes Intercom's AI pivot, its customer support agent Finn with 8,000+ customers, revenue approaching $100M, 2M resolutions per week, and a proprietary model outperforming frontier models for English text conversations. He notes he will not focus on Finn but on internal AI for engineering.

sections.title: Setting the 2x Goal
sections.summary: After dissatisfaction with Copilot, Cursor, and Augment, Intercom set a goal to double engineering throughput in a year, measured as code changes per R&D person. Brian acknowledges the metric's imperfections but emphasizes that genuine adoption should produce large throughput gains. He frames the goal as both wildly ambitious and unambitious given model trajectory.

sections.title: Organizational Change and Platform Choice
sections.summary: Brian covers leadership tactics: mandatory AI adoption in job descriptions, repeated messaging, celebrating wins, hackathons, AI immersion days, and a full-time 2x team. He explains choosing Claude Code as the single platform, arguing against multi-tool fragmentation via a multi-cloud analogy, and the vision of Claude acting as a senior engineer connected to everything.

sections.title: Onboarding Claude and Guiding Principles
sections.summary: Brian describes onboarding Claude with Rails conventions, architecture, testing, and security rules via skills, captures, guidance, and hooks. He details pushing internal plugins to laptops and the flywheel of updating guidance when Claude fails. He introduces principles: everything an engineer can do the agent must do, and engineers move up the stack like sysadmins transitioning to SREs.

sections.title: Skills Philosophy and Problem Framing
sections.summary: Brian explains Intercom's technically conservative approach of using single tools extremely well, focusing on small, high-quality, durable, testable skills with continuous improvement and backtesting. He introduces the principle of giving agents problems, not tasks, and recounts a security incident where Claude automatically discovered and used a data breach analysis skill he didn't know existed, completing in two minutes.

sections.title: AI Adoption Maturity and Results Data
sections.summary: Brian describes a maturity model for engineers progressing from using Claude Code for everything to optimizing the environment for agents. He presents results: PR throughput doubled in under a year after going all in on one tool starting in January, 17.6% auto-approval rate with SOC 2/ISO 27001/HIPAA compliance, code review becoming the new bottleneck, and backtesting to shape PRs toward safe auto-approvable changes.

sections.title: Observability, Defects, and Skills in Practice
sections.summary: Brian covers skill invocation observability via Honeycomb, session transcripts pulled into S3 for data mining, defects closing faster than ever, Stanford research confirming code quality gains, hundreds of plugin contributors, an example flaky-spec-fixing skill built through iterative feedback, CI melting under volume, Claude Code going viral outside engineering, and single-person team experiments using skills as a product manager.
